text:
A: Hiya! Can you hear me alright? I'm Jaspal, I'm in Derby.
B: Yes, I can hear you. Hi, I'm Klára. I'm in London, in Walthamstow.
A: Walthamstow, nice. I've only been through it on the way to a stag do, to be fair, so I can't say I know it. How did you find that puzzle thing at the start?
B: Erm, honestly, quite hard. I spent too long on the first one and then I had to rush the rest.
A: Same, same. And I teach economics, I'm supposed to be good at that sort of thing. I just sat there going round in circles. Don't tell my students.
B: You're a teacher? I guessed this, from the books behind you.
A: Ha, yeah, the books give it away. That and the pile of marking I'm pretending isn't there. It's a sixth form college on the edge of Derby, Business and Economics. I run the Young Enterprise group as well, so I've got seventeen-year-olds trying to sell me candles they've made in a garage.
B: Sorry, sixth form is sixteen to eighteen, yes?
A: Yeah, sixteen to eighteen. Best age, to be honest. They're old enough to argue with you properly. What about you, what do you do?
B: At the moment I'm at home with my son. He's three and a half. Before, I worked in a department store on Oxford Street, on the tills and the customer desk.
A: Oh right, so the dinosaur on the sofa in your photo...
B: Yes, that's his. He's just discovered dinosaurs and now he won't talk about anything else. This morning I had to be a diplodocus for one hour.
A: An hour? You're a better person than me. My partner's dog is the closest thing I've got, and he just eats socks.
B: Socks?
A: Socks, mate, it's a whole saga. Vet bill, the lot. Anyway, sorry, go on. Are you going back to work at some point, or...
B: I'm thinking about it. When he goes to nursery more hours. Maybe part-time, but not shop floor again. Something like reception, a GP surgery or a school office.
A: To be fair, if you've done a customer desk on Oxford Street you can do a GP reception standing on your head. That's the hardest job in Britain, that.
B: (laughs) Maybe. I was okay with complaints. I just listened, and I didn't promise things I couldn't do. People mostly want someone to listen.
A: That's it, isn't it? I'm the opposite, I promise everything and then panic. Where are you from originally, if you don't mind me asking?
B: Brno, in Czech Republic. I came in 2014. I was going to stay one year to improve my English, and then I met my husband.
A: One year, famous last words. My family were the same sort of thing, they meant to stop somewhere for a bit. We're Afghan Sikh, we came out of Kabul when I was little, spent about a year in Delhi, then ended up in Derby because my uncle had a shop. Thirty-odd years later, here I am, moaning about Derby County.
B: So you still speak, erm, Punjabi?
A: With my mum, yeah. And a bit of Dari. My English is miles better now though, she says my Punjabi sounds like a tourist's. Do you speak Czech with your son?
B: Yes, always Czech with him. My husband speaks a little, mostly food words and, erm, swearing.
A: The important stuff, then.
B: Yes, exactly. But I worry Matěj will answer me in English soon. Already he says "no, Mummy" in English.
A: Honestly, keep going with it. My cousins' kids lost theirs and they really regret it. It's like, once it goes...
